questions.question: A coal fire gives off its heat as its fuel joins with oxygen from the air. Lord Kelvin, one of the leading physicists of the 1800s, showed in 1862 that the Sun cannot be shining by any burning of that kind. What was his reason?
questions.answer: It would have burned out in a few thousand years
choices: It would have burned out in a few thousand years
It holds none of the oxygen that any burning needs
No fire could stay lit in the cold of empty space
Its ash would long since have smothered its fire
questions.context: Kelvin worked out that even the most powerful chemical burning would give only about 3,000 years of the Sun's heat, far too short for Earth's long history. The Sun does hold oxygen, the third most common element in it after hydrogen and helium, and a fire with oxygen of its own burns in empty space, as a rocket engine's does. Kelvin turned instead to the Sun's slow shrinking, which still gave it only some tens of millions of years.
questions.grade_note: Ninth-grade earth science asks how scientists know what powers the Sun, and Kelvin's sum is the classic case of ruling an idea out with numbers.

questions.question: Francis Aston, weighing atoms with new precision at Cambridge, found that a helium atom has a little less mass than four hydrogen atoms, about one part in 120 less. Arthur Eddington seized on the result in an address at Cardiff in August 1920. Shrinking, he argued, could never give the stars enough energy to shine as long as they do. What did he propose instead?
questions.answer: Stars shine by building helium out of hydrogen
choices: Stars shine by building helium out of hydrogen
Stars shine by breaking helium down into hydrogen
Stars shine by splitting heavy atoms such as uranium
Stars shine by the steady decay of radium inside them
questions.context: Lost mass means energy given out, so building a helium nucleus from four hydrogen nuclei turns about 0.7 percent of their mass into energy, while breaking helium apart would take energy in. The Sun is now known to fuse about 600 million tonnes of hydrogen every second, and about 4 million tonnes of its mass leave it as energy each second. Radium had been put forward as the Sun's fuel in 1903, but heavy atoms such as radium and uranium are only a tiny part of a Sun made almost wholly of hydrogen and helium.
questions.grade_note: Ninth graders learn that hydrogen fuses into helium in the Sun's core, and Eddington's reasoning from Aston's weighing is how that idea first arose.

questions.question: Ray Davis caught neutrinos, tiny particles that stream out of the Sun's core, in a tank of chlorine-rich fluid deep in a gold mine. He counted only a third as many as models of the Sun predicted. Neutrinos come in three kinds, and chlorine catches only one. Canada's Sudbury Neutrino Observatory found in 2001 and 2002 that all three kinds together match the models' total, though only a third are of Davis's kind. Which explanation of his shortfall did that leave standing?
questions.answer: They change kind on their way from the core
choices: They change kind on their way from the core
The Sun's core makes fewer than the models said
Most of them decay away on their way to Earth
Davis's tank had miscounted the one kind it caught
questions.context: The Sudbury Neutrino Observatory, 2,100 metres down a nickel mine in Ontario, watched 1,000 tonnes of heavy water. Its first results in 2001, set beside the count of the Super-Kamiokande detector in Japan, and its own count of all three kinds in 2002 showed the models' full number arriving, but only about a third as electron neutrinos, the one kind chlorine catches: the rest had changed kind on the way, which means neutrinos have mass. Most physicists had suspected Davis's count or the models of the core, and both were cleared; Davis won a share of the 2002 Nobel Prize in Physics, and SNO's Arthur McDonald a share of the 2015 prize.
questions.grade_note: Ninth-grade science teaches weighing rival explanations against a new result, and the missing solar neutrinos are a famous case where one measurement cleared both the experiment and the model of the Sun's core.

questions.question: Light from the Sun's surface crosses to Earth in about eight minutes. The energy it carries was made in the core long before: by most estimates its trip out took from about ten thousand to well over a hundred thousand years, most of that time in the dense layers around the core. Why is the trip out so slow?
questions.answer: The light is soaked up and sent off again in random directions
choices: The light is soaked up and sent off again in random directions
Hot atoms jostle their neighbours, passing it on by conduction
The Sun's strong gravity keeps pulling the light back down
It waits in the core until enough builds up to break out
questions.context: The gas around the core is so dense that light goes only a tiny way before an atom soaks it up and sends it off again in a new direction, so the energy zigzags outward like a lost walker; NASA's figure for that stretch is about 170,000 years. Rising and sinking gas then carries it through the outer third of the Sun much faster. Neutrinos from the core, which hardly touch the gas, cross the whole Sun in about two seconds.
questions.grade_note: Ninth graders learn that the Sun's energy slowly works outward from the core before it reaches Earth as radiation, and the zigzag of light is the reason.

questions.question: No one can bring a piece of the Sun into a laboratory to find its age. Yet astronomers give that age as about 4.6 billion years, and say the Sun is roughly halfway through its long, steady life. Where does the figure of 4.6 billion years come from?
questions.answer: Dating the Solar System's first solids, kept in meteorites
choices: Dating the Solar System's first solids, kept in meteorites
Dating the oldest rocks and crystals ever found on Earth
Timing how fast the Sun is shrinking, then counting back
Measuring how fast the Sun is cooling down, then counting back
questions.context: The first solids to form around the young Sun, grains rich in calcium and aluminium found in some meteorites, date by their radioactive elements to about 4.57 billion years, and the Sun's age is taken from them. Earth's oldest rocks are only about 4 billion years old and its oldest crystals about 4.4 billion, because most of its first crust has been melted and remade. Fusion has used up about half the fuel at the very centre of the Sun, which should keep up its steady fusion in the core, slowly growing brighter, for about 5 billion years more.
questions.grade_note: The Sun's age and its place halfway through its life are ninth-grade earth science, and the meteorites are how that age is known.

questions.question: Through a telescope with a proper solar filter, sunspots look black against the Sun's glowing face. Yet a sunspot is still thousands of degrees hot. Why does it look dark?
questions.answer: It is cooler, as its magnetism holds back heat from below
choices: It is cooler, as its magnetism holds back heat from below
It is cooler, as the fusion beneath it has died down
It is a gap in the glowing surface, showing a dark body below
It is the shadow of small moons crossing the Sun
questions.context: Strong magnetic fields, thousands of times stronger than the quiet Sun's, choke off the rising and sinking gas that carries heat up to the surface, so a spot's dark centre is some 1,500 degrees or more cooler than the surface around it, about 5,500 degrees Celsius, and looks dim beside it; cut out and seen on its own, a sunspot would shine brighter than the full Moon. Fusion happens only in the core, far below. Christoph Scheiner took the spots for small moons, but Galileo showed in 1613 that they lie on the Sun's face and turn with it, and William Herschel later took them for holes in a glowing outer layer, showing a solid body beneath.
questions.grade_note: Ninth-grade earth science teaches sunspots as cooler, magnetic regions of the Sun's surface.

questions.question: Heinrich Schwabe, a pharmacist in Dessau in Germany, watched the Sun on every clear day from 1826 to 1843. He hoped to catch an unknown planet, closer to the Sun than Mercury, crossing its face as a dark dot, and he noted down every sunspot he saw. He never found the planet. What did his record of the sunspots show?
questions.answer: Their number rose and fell over about ten years
choices: Their number rose and fell over about ten years
Their number grew steadily over the seventeen years
Their number rose and fell with Mercury's trips round the Sun
Their number rose and fell with Earth's seasons
questions.context: Schwabe reported a probable ten-year period in 1843; few noticed at first, but Rudolf Wolf took up regular counts, and the Royal Astronomical Society gave Schwabe its Gold Medal in 1857. The cycle is now measured at about 11 years on average, from just under 10 to just over 12, and it is a cycle of the Sun's magnetism: about every 11 years the Sun's magnetic poles swap places. Solar flares come most often near the cycle's peak.
questions.grade_note: The 11-year sunspot cycle is ninth-grade earth science, and Schwabe's patient count is how it was found.

questions.question: Richard Carrington was drawing sunspots in England just before noon on 1 September 1859 when two patches of brilliant white light flared up among them, then faded within five minutes. About 17 hours later auroras glowed as far south as Cuba, and telegraph lines across Europe and North America threw sparks. On one line operators unhooked their batteries and still sent messages for two hours. What drove the current?
questions.answer: Earth's changing magnetic field drove it along the wires
choices: Earth's changing magnetic field drove it along the wires
Charged particles from the Sun fell straight onto the wires
Charge left by the batteries still filled the long wires
Lightning from thunderclouds along the line struck the wires
questions.context: A cloud of magnetised gas thrown out by the Sun struck Earth and set its magnetic field swinging, and a changing magnetic field drives currents along long wires, enough to shock operators and set paper alight. Carrington suspected that the flare had caused the storm but would not claim it from one case, writing that 'one swallow does not make a summer'. Flares are now known to be sudden releases of magnetic energy stored around sunspots, and a storm in March 1989 blacked out the power grid of Quebec for up to nine hours.
questions.grade_note: Ninth-grade earth science teaches solar flares and space weather, and the Carrington Event applies the ninth-grade rule that a changing magnetic field drives a current.

questions.question: Margaret Burbidge, Geoffrey Burbidge, William Fowler and Fred Hoyle set out in 1957 how stars forge the chemical elements, over their long lives and in the supernova blasts that scatter what they made into space, where new stars and planets form from it. Most of the matter in a human body was made in stars. Which of the body's atoms were not?
choices: The hydrogen in its water
The oxygen in its water
The carbon in its muscles
The iron in its blood
questions.context: Hydrogen was made in the Big Bang, with helium and a little lithium, before any star shone, and it is the fuel that stars fuse into everything heavier, so the hydrogen in every water molecule in a body is older than the stars. The oxygen bonded to it in that water, like the body's carbon, was made by fusion inside stars, and much of its iron in supernovae long ago. Hydrogen is only about a tenth of a body's mass, though it makes up about six of every ten of its atoms.
questions.grade_note: Ninth-grade earth science teaches that stars make the heavier elements and scatter them, so the atoms of living things were made in stars, and hydrogen is the exception.

questions.question: At the very centre of the Sun, at about 15 million degrees Celsius, fusion runs slowly. Models put the heat it makes there at about 280 watts in each cubic metre, about as much as an active compost heap gives off and less than a person's body does, size for size. Why does the Sun shine so brightly all the same?
questions.answer: Its core holds a vast amount of gas, all of it fusing
choices: Its core holds a vast amount of gas, all of it fusing
Its vast outer layers make far more heat than its core
Its gravity squeezes out far more heat than fusion
It still glows with heat stored up since its birth
questions.context: Fusion happens only in the core, which reaches about a fifth to a quarter of the way from the centre to the surface, and that ball of gas is so vast that its slow output, cubic metre by cubic metre, adds up to all the Sun's light. Without fusion, the Sun's stored heat and slow shrinking together could have kept it shining only some tens of millions of years, as Lord Kelvin found.
questions.grade_note: Ninth-grade earth science teaches that fusion in the Sun's core powers it, and weighing the core's slow rate against its vast size is honest reasoning about how that power adds up.

The judge's second rival, annihilation of whole atoms, was not used, because Eddington himself raised it in 1917 and leaned to it later (F38), so it could be defended as his proposal. dropped.question: Arthur Eddington's critics had a hard objection to his account of how stars shine. Atomic nuclei all carry a positive charge, and their electric push stands like a wall between them: in the Sun's core a typical one has hundreds of times too little energy to climb it and get close enough to another to fuse. Eddington told them to go and find a hotter place. What answered the critics?
dropped.why: Judge (high, grade and tell): the key, quantum tunnelling, is beyond 9th grade and outside the unit's scope (HS-ESS1-1 leaves out sub-atomic detail of the Sun's fusion), what is left is already keyed by fission-fusion-and-mass-energy ('Only fast nuclei get close despite pushing each other away'), and the stem's own words ruled out two choices. Dropped as the judge and the lead said; replaced by the core's slow power density, which also carries the core's 15 million degrees.
